analysis.title: What Matters Today: AI Hyperscalers Energy, State Elections Power Utilities, Treasury Refunding (5 Nov 2026)
key_insights: AI/energy: legislative restrictions on data center build-out are hard to quantify, particularly in the out years, but building will become more expensive, complicated and slower. Multiples have compressed sharply, positioning was already derisked and another wave of selling followed. Some moves looked capitulatory.

The market is pricing peak CapEx growth. The author does not think it must also price an outright spending deceleration, since delayed projects are not cancelled demand. Delays could create an inventory glut across chips, turbines, cooling and electrical equipment.

The author asks whether the industry has overordered against an energisation schedule it can no longer deliver, and whether that undermines semiconductor capacity expansion at ASML and TSMC. The stated risk is an inventory cycle, not demand destruction.

Compute owners: existing energised compute becomes more valuable. Hyperscalers potentially earn better economics on scarce capacity, and constrained expansion implies less CapEx and higher FCF. Amazon rallied despite last week's FCF concerns.
Scarcity favors owners of capacity and is potentially disastrous for companies whose valuations depend on building it.

Energy: the physical oil market has collapsed. Physical Brent traded at a $2.87 discount to Dated Brent yesterday, reportedly a record extreme, versus a premium of more than $20/bl three weeks ago. November CFDs and the front three weeks of Dated Brent are in contango.

Prompt Brent fell about $8.50 across the session and after-hours to about $94. Oil is pricing as if the war is over, and some argue fair value is below $70. Physical scarcity is disappearing ahead of any confirmed resolution. The author calls this supportive for rates, consumer and underowned assets, but worries the market may be ahead of itself given weekend escalation risk (credit: Rich Privo).

State elections: GS believes Democratic wins could raise near-term uncertainty around data center development, particularly in Texas and Georgia, which remain important longer-term load growth markets.
Texas: the gubernatorial outcome could drive negative reactions in Buy-rated VST, NRG, SRE and XEL and Neutral-rated CEG and AEP.
Georgia: the PSC election outcome could be negative for Neutral-rated SO.
Ohio: the gubernatorial outcome could be less constructive for Buy-rated FE and Neutral-rated AEP, with more limited impact on Buy-rated DUK.
California: GS awaits clarity on a potential special legislative session before November 15. If called, the outcome could be positive for Buy-rated PCG and SRE and Neutral-rated EIX.

Treasury refunding: 4Q26 marketable borrowing estimate is $618bn versus GS projection of $571bn. The 1Q27 projection is $800bn versus GS $713bn, driven mainly by a TGA cash balance target of $1tn versus GS assumption of $900bn.

Treasury emphasized demand and cost effectiveness when evaluating issuance shifts. Debt managers noted growing private-sector and SOMA demand for bills, signaling comfort with bill absorption, though TBAC noted increasing price sensitivity amid sluggish MMF AUM growth.
GS expects auction size increases to be limited to the 2-to-10y part of the curve. The baseline is unchanged long-end auction sizes, with risks skewed toward modest reductions.
